data.title: Donut Lab Reveals Amazing Performance Tests
data.description:
Donut Lab revealed its solid-state battery to the world at CES 2026, to the amazement of many and to the dismay of others shocked by their achievement and performance claims. No other company has a practical fully solid-state battery in production as of this writing. Many, like Quantumscape, have tried for many years, only to find that limitations exist, like the need for extreme mechanical pressures required to maintain contact between cathode and electrode. Such measures require bulky and heavy support, obviating benefits of solid-state operation. Many have resorted to semi-solid-state as a compromise. Semi-solid-state batteries were used by NIO for battery swapping, but they ceased operation since cost and other practical factors proved unsatisfactory.

Not long after Donut Lab’s solid-state battery presentation, howls of derision and a cavalcade of insults and skepticism followed. Much of the criticism, unsurprisingly, came from established players in the battery market with vested interests in legacy batteries, companies which failed to produce a practical solid-state battery, proving Upton Sinclair’s dictum: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends on him not understanding it.” Just because it is new and innovative does not mean it is real and it works, and it is prudent to request data. Some waited for data to decide, while others impatiently jumped to conclusions. In this case, in response to the many critics who said it was impossible and a scam, an unusual amount of proof beyond normal practice in the battery industry was provided. It’s not that large legacy battery makers do not provide proof. They usually provide data sheets carefully constructed to show their products in the best light for intended applications, and the boring engineering details are left in the background that show the limits. Nothing to see here, just the usual. They seldom provide such extended public proof, such as disassembly and extensive tests by independent testers.

Nail Tests

In particular with batteries, some tests are demonstrated to showcase best performance in a more dramatic way, like nail penetration tests. These are important tests and do show some of the safety attributes specific to different battery chemistries. Nail penetration and other safety tests are now standardized requirements for rechargeable batteries in China, a good development ensuring public safety and aiding battery use. Donut Lab’s battery was tested at 12V terminal voltage and then did nail penetration tests that showed absolutely no fire, smoke, or explosion and very little change in temperature, a very boring and safe result. NMC produces a more exciting display with flame and high temperatures, while LFP is less exciting and produces no fire, but some smoke. Sodium-ion batteries also produce unexciting nail tests. That set of Donut Lab tests also showed that the battery was bipolar, because the terminal voltage was above 12V and batteries with different numbers of layers showed several different voltages.

Incontrovertible Solid-State Proof

Good things are worth the wait, and Donut Lab has delivered new data. The latest tests prove the battery is solid-state and the measured gravimetric energy density is 409 Wh/kg. The volumetric energy density result is 804 Wh/l. Proof of solid-state was provided in several ways. The batteries can be made in bipolar format. That means the cells are stacked on top of each other within the package, producing a wide variety of external voltages depending on the number of cells within the package. This is impossible with a liquid electrolyte in one package. Liquid electrolytes can flow freely among all cells in the same package and ions can shuttle between multiple cells spoiling desired serial ion flow through each stacked cell. A solid-state electrolyte can stay in place between cell cathode and anode without providing a path for ions between other cells. A liquid electrolyte bipolar battery must provide separate isolated chambers for each cell electrolyte, making practical construction difficult and unwieldy. The advantage of bipolar construction is that current flows through a thin depth and over a large area, providing less resistance and requiring less electrode material than single cells constructed in a pack, increasing the ratio of active material and lowering costs. In pack construction, fewer modules are used and external conductors are reduced. The net effect is higher density at both battery and pack level, even comparing to cell-to-pack technology. In a remarkable demonstration, the cell was disassembled and showed internal construction consisted of repeated layers. There was no internal mechanical isolation between layers within the package. The layers are connected electrically by stacking. This leaves no doubt that the battery is bipolar and solid-state.

Social Media Got It Wrong

While I already recognized that liquid electrolyte NMC cells could not survive operation at 100°C undamaged, that was not enough proof for some that insisted it was an NMC cell. I debunked the notion that a cell produces a unique fingerprint by showing that other cells produced similar full charge and discharge open circuit voltages. Others have gone on to add to this. The unique fingerprint theory is wrong. It is possible to alter voltage characteristics by doping and other means. Bipolar operation brings into question whether the batteries previously tested were single cell or multiple stacked cells. Bipolar operation and disassembly show the connections create a single-stacked battery, an impossibility for a liquid electrolyte NMC battery. It cannot be assumed the previously packaged battery tested was a single cell. Despite all of this, incredibly, some have mistakenly concluded that there is no proof the battery is solid-state. They are wrong. Their conclusion that Donut Lab has no credibility is equally wrong and exposes their own credibility.

An Overlooked Matter and Story — Process

While solid-state construction and extraordinary battery performance gain headlines, process methods seem to gain little attention. I explained why the manufacturing process may be more revolutionary than solid-state operation. For those studying the field, it is no secret that printing has been a major focus for the solid-state manufacturing process. There are many studies on that. Investigations have shown that CT-coatings is the source of nano pastes used with silk screen printers. A process using nanopastes and printers may not require machinery in sealed vacuum chambers, removing toxic, flammable solvents like legacy liquid electrolyte lithium batteries do.

Donut Lab says its batteries also do not require formation. Formation is a last step in battery manufacture. Batteries undergo first full charge in this step. It forms the solid electrolyte interface (SEI) layer. Cells are warehoused in racks for up to a week, requiring large amounts of storage space. This step is the most expensive part of legacy battery manufacture. Together with the large sealed rooms and toxic vapor recovery, legacy battery manufacturing is achingly capital and operating cost intensive. Vapor recovery also requires large amounts of electricity. A 1 GWh factory can cost a billion dollars. By comparison, printed solid-state battery manufacture without expensive space-consuming formation and containment rooms is estimated to cost an order of magnitude less. Together with cheaper material costs than NMC, and easily sourced and widely available materials, printed battery manufacturing could pose a real threat to vested interests with huge sunk costs that are now in danger of becoming stranded assets. There are now several companies entertaining solid-state processing by the new printing method.

Conclusion and What is Next

From this, no conclusions can be drawn about what the cell chemistry is, but we can conclude the batteries can achieve over 400 Wh/kg and 800 Wh/l in packaged form, and are indeed solid-state, with other benefits — in all, a stunning performance result. So far, other performance claims have been verified, leaving only two important remaining performance claims unsupported, cycle life and -30°C energy retention.

The results seem anticlimactic after the rancorous critics’ responses, but there they are. It is beginning to look like critics that bet money may need to get out their checkbooks or wallets. The hoopla and pressure of social media clicks has subsided for a while. We will see whether critics own up. No doubt, some critics will persist even when shown to be wrong. The battery has proved to be solid-state, not a legacy NMC battery, and bipolar capable. Bipolar operation was not a focus early on. We are awaiting demonstrations of low temperature operation and cycle life, but now that the other claims have been proven, the battery is already remarkable. I don’t think competitors can sleep easy waiting for the final tests. There may be considerable agitation and acrimony in boardroom meetings upon hearing the latest news. I expect the industrial spies will be out in droves after this, if they are not already. It is too late to tamp down interest in this battery with disparaging rumors. Things are getting serious. There is too much proof. The test results matter. There is a real battery with astonishing performance. The ramifications of these test results deserve sober consideration.

data.title: Hyundai Motor Group Partners with Oman to Drive Green Mobility Transition under Oman Vision 2040
data.description:
• Hyundai Motor Group Signs Historic Partnership Agreements with Oman’s Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology
  • The Group Teams Up with Mwasalat to Launch Oman’s First Hydrogen City Bus in Muscat
  • Oman Oil Marketing Company and EV Charging Brand EVO Join Forces with the Group to Build 240kW Ultra-Fast EV Charger Near Muscat
  • Hyundai Kefico Formalizes EV Charging Test Cooperation with EVO Through New MOU

Hyundai Motor Group (the Group) today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Oman’s Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology (MTCIT) at the Gulf Green Mobility Forum, launching cooperation in smart city development and eco-friendly mobility. Through this agreement, the Group positions itself as a key partner in Oman’s national smart city strategy under Vision 2040. The partnership runs for an initial one-year term, subject to automatic renewal.

The same visit also saw separate agreements signed with Oman’s public transport and energy sectors, including a pilot program for Oman’s first hydrogen city bus and the deployment of an ultra-fast EV charger in Muscat.

“We are delighted to establish strategic partnerships with MTCIT today. HMG is committed to helping turn Oman’s Vision 2040 ambitions into tangible outcomes through collaboration in smart cities and future mobility.” —Hokeun Chung, Executive Vice President, Head of Future Strategy Division, Hyundai Motor Group

What Does the MTCIT Partnership Cover?

The Omani government is advancing state-led smart city development under Vision 2040, with flagship projects including Sultan Haitham City. The MOU with the Group establishes a framework for cooperation spanning smart city development and eco-friendly mobility, including electric and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles. Through this partnership, the Group positions itself as a partner in Oman’s sustainable urban transition and carbon neutrality efforts.

How Will Oman’s First Hydrogen City Bus Operate?

Oman’s national transport operator Mwasalat has signed a Pilot Agreement (PA) with the Group to deploy Oman’s first hydrogen city bus, the ELEC CITY Fuel Cell, on public transit routes in Muscat. Rather than a short-term technology demonstration, the initiative is designed as an actual passenger transportation service. The 24-seat hydrogen fuel cell bus will run as part of a pilot service from the third quarter of 2026 through the third quarter of 2027.

Where Will the New Ultra-Fast EV Charger Be Installed?

OOMCO, the energy distribution subsidiary of Oman’s national energy group OQ, and EV charging brand EVO have each signed MOUs with Hyundai Motor Group and Hyundai Kefico, respectively, to build and operate a 240kW DC ultra-fast charger at a service station in Halban, near Muscat.

What Happens After the Pilot Programs?

This cooperation between Hyundai Motor Group and its Omani partners is not intended as a one-off pilot project. Throughout the hydrogen bus pilot, Mwasalat will evaluate the vehicle’s reliability under real-world driving conditions, its operational efficiency across daily transit routes, and its environmental performance compared to conventional diesel buses. For the EV charging infrastructure, the partners will assess charging performance, user demand, and commercial feasibility to lay the groundwork for future expansion.

Based on these results, measured against pre-agreed key performance indicators (KPIs), the participating organizations will explore expanding services and formalizing procurement across Oman.

data.title: Geely’s BEV Sales Grow 29% in August
data.description:
It hasn’t been the best of years for electric vehicle sales in China. But it has been the best year by far for Chinese EV sales abroad. It looks like Geely is following that trend.

The Chinese automaker, one of the largest in the world, had modest sales growth in August, but significant BEV sales growth, and enormous export growth.

The Geely brand was up 5% year over year in August, its Lynk & Co arm was down a whopping 37%, and its Zeekr arm was up 110%. The net result from the drastically different results of the two EV brands was an increase of more than 9,000 sales.

Overall, Geely’s BEV sales rose from 93,362 units in August 2025 to 120,590 units in August 2026, a 29% increase. (Plugin hybrid sales increase modestly, by 2%, from 53,985 units to 55,287 units.) But here’s the whammy: the company’s exports grew 205%, from 36,077 in August 2025 to 110,094 in August 2026. This is the big global trend at the moment — Chinese automakers shipping a lot more cars (largely EVs) to other countries.

Oh, by the way, Geely’s overall sales grew by 8% year over year, from 250,167 in August 2025 to 270,194 in August 2026. Yes, if exports grew by about 74,000 units and overall sales grew by about 20,000 units, that means the company’s sales in its home market of China were down by about 54,000 units.

(Oh, by the way, I was planning to cover BYD’s export data and trends this week, but the company has decided not to publish that data this month for some reason. I need to look into it more….)

data.title: Hyundai Motor & KOICA Launch “Hyundai-KOICA NextGen” to Train Ghana’s Future Automotive Talent
data.description:
• Hyundai Motor and KOICA launch ‘Hyundai-KOICA NextGen’ in Ghana to train skilled automotive technicians and strengthen the country’s workforce development system
  • Under KOICA’s Inclusive Business Solution (IBS) program, which links corporate resources and strategies with official development assistance (ODA), Hyundai Motor and KOICA will jointly fund the KRW 5 billion project over five years on a 5:5 matching basis
  • New public-private partnership will support 405 teachers and students through curriculum development and two new education centers
  • Project builds on Hyundai Motor’s commitment to Creating Shared Value (CSV) through its global ‘Hyundai Continue’ initiative

Hyundai Motor Company and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) today officially launched ‘Hyundai-KOICA NextGen’ in Ghana, the first project under Hyundai Motor’s global Creating Shared Value (CSV) initiative, ‘Hyundai Continue,’ focused on technology education and workforce development.

Developed under KOICA’s Inclusive Business Solution (IBS) program and implemented in collaboration with Plan International Korea and Plan International Ghana, the project aims to strengthen Ghana’s automotive workforce by training skilled maintenance technicians and building sustainable industry-academia collaboration.

The launch ceremony was held in Accra on September 3 and attended by key representatives from Hyundai Motor, KOICA and partner organizations, including Jae Sun Yoo, Team Leader of Hyundai Motor M.East & Africa Headquarters Marketing & Communication Team; Dongwan Woo, Country Director of the KOICA Ghana Office; Ing. Dr. Eric Kofi Adzroe, Director-General of Ghana TVET Service; and Frederick Tei-Nobi, Acting Country Director of Plan International Ghana.

“With the launch of this project, Hyundai Motor will continue its technology talent development program to strengthen the competitiveness of the automotive industry. Through an updated curriculum covering the latest developments in hybrid and electric vehicle maintenance, we are equipping Ghanaian youth with future-ready skills and empowering them to play a meaningful role in the continued growth of Ghana’s automotive industry. We look forward to seeing the lasting impact this project will have on thousands of young people and their communities.” —Joongsun Ko, Senior Vice President of Corporate Strategy & Planning at Hyundai Motor Company

“This project translates the shared commitment of Korea and Ghana into practical action by connecting skills development with industry needs, employment and entrepreneurship. By bringing together Hyundai Motor’s technical expertise, KOICA’s development cooperation expertise, Plan International’s experience in youth empowerment and the leadership of our Ghanaian partner institutions, we aim to create new opportunities for young people and help build a stronger, more future-ready automotive sector in Ghana.” —Dongwan Woo, Country Director of the KOICA Ghana Office

“For Plan International Ghana, this partnership is closely aligned with our commitment to creating opportunities that enable young people to build secure, productive and fulfilling futures. We are proud to be part of this journey, and we look forward to working with all our partners to ensure that Hyundai-KOICA NextGen delivers meaningful and sustainable results.” —Frederick Tei-Nobi, Acting Country Director, Plan International Ghana

Why Was Hyundai NextGen Launched in Ghana?

Ghana is emerging as a key automotive hub in West Africa, but limitations in its workforce development system and barriers to youth employment are restricting the country’s industrial competitiveness.

A baseline assessment conducted during the project planning phase identified several areas where additional support and investment are needed. For example, 80 percent of educational institutions lack an up-to-date curriculum and 70 percent of educational equipment currently in use is more than 10 years old. Furthermore, only a quarter of instructors possess electronic diagnostic knowledge and just 12.5 percent have experience with EVs.

These challenges have highlighted the need to better align workforce skills with evolving industry demands. Employer satisfaction with technical education graduates stands below 40 percent, while formal industry-academia cooperation and support for vulnerable youth also remain limited.

What Is the Hyundai–KOICA NextGen Project?

The project centers on three main areas:

Establishment of two maintenance technology education centers: Providing training to teachers on the updated curriculum, with trained teachers disseminating knowledge to students at nearby technical schools. The centers will feature hands-on practical maintenance facilities for comprehensive skill development.

  • Curriculum development: Enhancing the existing internal combustion engine curriculum and introducing new hybrid and electric vehicle maintenance curricula, both to be certified by the Commission for Technical and Vocational Educational Training (CTVET), under Ghana’s Ministry of Education.
  • Employment and startup support: Providing scholarships and internship opportunities for vulnerable young students, hosting annual job fairs and delivering startup education and consulting services to facilitate the transition from education to employment and entrepreneurship.

The Hyundai-KOICA NextGen Project is expected to support a total of 405 local youth and teachers through strengthened technical education, internship opportunities and pathways to employment and entrepreneurship.

What Does This Mean for the Future of Ghana’s Automotive Industry?

Hyundai-KOICA NextGen Project addresses outdated curricula, limited teacher competency and aging equipment. It is designed to build a sustainable pipeline of skilled technicians who can meet the demands of a modernizing automotive sector, including the shift toward hybrids and EVs.

The project builds on Hyundai Motor’s ongoing commitment to global CSV projects under the global Hyundai Continue initiative, reinforcing the company’s mission to create lasting social value in the communities where it operates.

data.title: Hydrogen Kept Failing The Test — And Getting Another Test
data.description:
In 2023, a senior executive responsible for decarbonizing a major transportation company asked me, with some exasperation, what drove the “madness on hydrogen.” Hydrogen proposals kept arriving for applications where the energy balance and economics looked dreadful. That conversation became What Drives This Madness On Hydrogen?, an attempt to explain why enthusiasm persisted despite increasingly obvious problems.

Three years later, I would change the weighting of my answer. Confirmation bias, familiarity and loss aversion were real, but I put them too close to the beginning of the causal chain. The more important question is why companies, governments and institutions acquired such strong reasons to keep hydrogen politically viable that adverse evidence repeatedly failed to stop the pathway.

The harder question is what kept hydrogen alive after the technical case had weakened. The full TFIE Strategy Briefing retrospective follows the fossil-fuel and automotive incentives, the institutional evidence and the places where stopping rules disappeared.

The constraints themselves were not obscure. A 2003 thermodynamic critique of the hydrogen economy traced the electricity required to make, compress, transport, store and use hydrogen and showed why it was intrinsically much more energy intensive than using electricity directly. That basic disadvantage never went away. Green hydrogen could be made with renewable electricity, but doing so did not make it cheap enough to compete broadly with direct electrification.

The economics reinforced the physics. Electrolysis wants extremely cheap electricity, but an expensive industrial plant also wants high utilization. The cheapest wind and solar hours are intermittent. Run only during those hours and the plant sits idle much of the year; raise utilization and electricity becomes more expensive through overbuilding, transmission, storage or purchases in higher-priced periods. I described that tradeoff in 2022 as the economic seesaw of green hydrogen. Meanwhile the electrolyzer stack was routinely confused with the whole plant, which also needs transformers, rectifiers, water treatment, cooling, purification, compression, piping, controls, safety systems and substantial grid infrastructure. By 2025, observed project costs were badly outrunning major institutional forecasts.

If those constraints were already visible, continuing enthusiasm requires an explanation other than technical ignorance. The answer becomes clearer when hydrogen is viewed not just as an energy carrier, but as a way of preserving the value of existing assets, skills and institutions.

Gas companies own reserves, pipelines, processing infrastructure and subsurface expertise whose strategic value declines sharply in a world where heating, transportation and much of industry electrify directly. Hydrogen offered an alternative future in which gas could become blue hydrogen, pipelines could remain molecule pipelines, carbon capture could gain another market and existing engineering competencies could stay valuable deep into the 2030s and 2040s. The people making those decisions were not incapable of understanding hydrogen economics. Much of the relevant engineering sat directly inside their organizations.

Legacy automakers faced a similar problem. Battery-electric vehicles shift competitive advantage away from combustion chambers, injection systems, transmissions, emissions controls and engine factories toward cells, motors, power electronics, software and high-voltage architecture. Hydrogen combustion and e-fuels offered a future in which more of the incumbent industrial system remained useful. Protecting workers, suppliers and industrial regions is a legitimate policy concern. Preserving inefficient propulsion technologies to avoid confronting that transition is something different.

Governments then created another layer of commitment. Once hydrogen targets, subsidy programs, manufacturing plans and infrastructure strategies existed, entire ecosystems organized around them. The European Court of Auditors’ review of EU hydrogen policy found that major targets had been set without sufficiently robust analysis, yet those targets had already shaped billions of euros of investment decisions and years of industrial planning.

That is where the absence of a stopping rule becomes important. Expensive hydrogen justified production subsidies. Missing customers justified demand support. Underused filling stations justified more stations and vehicles. Pipelines without committed throughput were justified as infrastructure needed to stimulate the production and demand that would eventually fill them. Each intervention could be defended on its own while the original question — whether hydrogen should serve the application at all — quietly disappeared.

Hydrogen still has important uses. Existing ammonia, methanol and chemical production must be decarbonized, and some iron-production pathways may create additional demand. Those are applications where the molecule itself has value and can justify paying the unavoidable premium for low-carbon hydrogen. They never required hydrogen to become a general-purpose substitute for electricity in heating, road transportation or routine energy storage.

That is what has changed most in my view of the hydrogen boom. Cognitive biases helped people defend positions they had already taken, but the commitments came first: reserves, pipelines, factories, supplier networks, public targets, budgets and careers. Much of the hydrogen detour was not inexplicable madness at all. It was rational organizational self-interest producing irrational energy policy, compounded by institutions that repeatedly failed to force the original proposition back onto the table when the evidence turned against it.

data.title: Mitsubishi Continues Bet on PHEV Muscle as Outlander Makes Philippine Return
EU Heavy-Duty Vehicle Transition Needs Renewed Political Momentum
data.description:
IRU and T&E are calling on European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to launch a strategic dialogue on heavy-duty vehicle decarbonisation, as key EU rules head for review and rising energy and cost pressures add urgency to getting the transition right.

Europe’s road transport sector is under growing pressure. The energy and geopolitical crisis triggered by the wars in Iran and Ukraine has pushed diesel prices sharply higher and has reinforced concerns over Europe’s energy security. Climate change-driven extreme weather is increasingly affecting communities and livelihoods, disrupting transport operations and putting infrastructure under growing strain.

To meet this challenge, IRU and T&E — in a joint letter to President von der Leyen — are calling for renewed political leadership and a high-level dialogue bringing together transport operators, vehicle manufacturers, infrastructure and energy providers and civil society to tackle the practical and economic barriers holding back a rapid transition to zero emission trucks.

IRU EU Advocacy Director Raluca Marian said, “The transition of heavy-duty transport needs renewed political momentum at the highest level. The EU has set a clear direction, but delivering it will require EU and national efforts to go hand in hand. A strategic dialogue led by President von der Leyen would send an important signal that the transition of trucks, buses and coaches remains an EU priority. It would bring together the key actors to identify what is still holding back deployment and where action is most urgently needed. Operators are the ones investing in and running these vehicles every day. Their operational and economic realities need to be at the heart of the decisions shaping the next phase of the transition.”

T&E Executive Director William Todts said, “The diesel crisis is a wake up call for Europe. We must rapidly reduce our dependence on imported oil and the single best way to do that is by scaling up electric trucks run on clean, homegrown electricity. The EU is preparing action on charging and CO2 standards. What we need to succeed is a transparent, inclusive process with all the key players around the table.”

The call comes ahead of reviews of two key EU laws: the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), which drives the rollout of charging and hydrogen infrastructure, and the Heavy-Duty Vehicle CO₂ Standards, which set CO₂ reduction targets for new heavy-duty vehicles.

IRU and T&E stress that progress will also depend on sufficient grid and charging capacity, competitive energy prices, financing and demand for zero-emission transport.

Featured photo by European Parliament via Flickr (CC BY 2.0 license).

data.title: Powering Sovereignty
data.description:
How electrification can lead our transport transition away from polluting fuel imports in the EU post-2030 Renewable Energy Framework.

With the recurrent energy crisis affecting Europe’s energy supply, Europe’s post-2030 Renewable Energy Framework must do more than just increase the share of renewables in transport.

It must also rethink its dependency pathways on imported fuels.

One way to do so is to cut the amount of energy the sector needs, which will inevitably reduce fuel imports and will make the transport system less exposed to oil and bio-feedstocks supply shocks.

Reflected in AccelerateEU and the Electrification Action Plan, this year we have seen a paradigm shift resulting from the energy crisis. Direct electrification is increasingly recognised as the clearest and more ambitious way to cut energy demand, while allowing higher competitiveness, security of supply, and lower energy prices.

In transport, every electric car, van and truck reduces demand for imported fuels, making electrification primarily an economic and energy security policy with emissions reduction a co-benefit. By combining much greater energy efficiency with increasingly domestically produced renewable electricity, electrification offers the most direct route to European transport energy sovereignty.

Weakening the current car CO2 standards would slow electrification and increase fuel demand, requiring greater use of fossil fuels, Annex IX advanced and waste biofuels, and e-fuels. Faster EV uptake, on the other hand — driven by corporate fleet standards and scrappage schemes, for example — would cut overall fuel demand and reduce reliance on imports.

A higher headline transport renewable energy target cannot, on its own, deliver greater energy sovereignty. Without ambitious electrification measures, the target could be met through greater reliance on scarce and imported fuels, while leaving Europe exposed to volatile global energy markets.

To ensure the future Renewable Energy Framework becomes an energy security and sovereignty tool, policymakers must look beyond the headline renewable energy transport target. What matters is not only how high the target is, but how it is met. A higher RES-T target must therefore be accompanied by ambitious electrification measures and a correspondingly higher contribution from renewable electricity.

All in all, the 2040 RES-T must power sovereignty by accelerating the shift towards cleaner and more efficient transport, anchored in domestically produced energy.

Here’s what the EU must prioritise in the upcoming Energy Union Framework for the decade ahead:

  • Put direct electrification at the core of the EU’s post-2030 Renewable Energy Framework and energy sovereignty strategy by requiring renewable electricity to account for at least half of the total RES-T target in 2040.
  • Preserve the 4x multiplier renewable electricity but apply it across all transport modes and ensure that any increase in the RES-T target is matched by a higher electricity contribution, rather than greater reliance on scarce biofuels.
  • Set a transport fossil oil demand phase out target and KPI in the post-2030 energy union framework for cutting import dependencies from 93% in 2025 to less than 75% in 2040, thereby reducing Europe’s exposure to oil shocks and strengthening energy security.
  • Defend credible and robust car CO2 standards as proposed under the European Green Deal, rejecting loopholes that allow a high share of biofuels and e-fuels to substitute for direct electrification in road transport.
  • Make the crediting mechanism in RED Article 25 mandatory across transport segments, covering public and private EV charging, depot charging for heavy-duty vehicles, rail, shore-side electricity and electric ships, as well as electric and hybrid aircraft to reward the use of renewable electricity.
  • Allow operators of charging infrastructure connected directly to renewable power generation via Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), to claim full renewable-electricity use above the national grid average for renewable electricity (RES-E).
  • Reflect the limited role of Annex IX biofuels in the post-2030 Energy Framework, by factoring constrained availability and the cascading-use principle, maintaining strict sustainability safeguards, such as Annex IX list and caps, and avoiding a surge in imports that heighten traceability and fraud risks.

Download the full briefing. Article from T&E.

data.title: It’s Game On As Ford Fathom Steals Thunder From Tesla Cybercab Launch
data.description:
The forthcoming Ford Fathom electric pickup truck is aimed squarely at stealing market share from industry leader Tesla one way or another, and the gloves are off. This week, fresh news broke around the Fathom right in the middle of the leadup to a major new promotional event for the Tesla Cybercab robotaxi in Texas. Of course, pickup trucks and robotaxis are two different things, but Ford has spotted a fresh opportunity to battle for the hearts and minds of the EV-buying public

The PR Wars Are On: Ford Fathom Vs. Tesla Cybercab

Ford has been diligently promoting the new all-electric pickup truck since last year, despite the headlong downward plunge in EV sales following the election of US President Donald Trump to a second term in office. The Ford Fathom will be the first vehicle to roll off Ford’s new purpose-built “Universal” EV platform, based around a cost-cutting, labor-saving, tree-like manufacturing process rather than the traditional gasmobile assembly line model.

The Fathom will also be available at the relatively affordable price point of under $30,000. Though prototypes have been hidden behind an elaborately plastered camouflage, an enterprising dealer in Palestine, Texas has been displaying a Fathom-adjacent pickup truck on its website since mid-August (pictured above).

In the latest news, at 7:00 pm on September 2 the Wall Street Journal scooped word — from an anonymous source — that Ford is aiming to sell 100,000 Fathoms in its first year of production, which is just around the corner.

“If it meets Ford’s targets, Fathom would instantly become one of the top-selling EVs in the U.S. in the first year of its production,” enthused WSJ reporter Ryan Felton.

In the meantime, Tesla CEO Elon Musk has made sure that the automotive press is primed and ready for today’s Cybercab event in Austin, Texas. The teasing revved up in earnest on August 17, when the news organization The Information reported that Tesla was prepping to launch the autonomous, car-without-a-steering-wheel Cybercab into its Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

As is typical of Musk and Tesla, though, the specifics of the event have not been forthcoming, and evidently the launched was pushed into September.

“Tesla offered riders of its ​current robotaxi fleet based on its Model Y a chance to join a ‘Cybercab Launch Event,’ but it has given no details about what kind of launch is planned,” Reuters reported on September 2.

“Tesla has been marketing ​the event as ‘Exclusive Access: Cybercab’ in posts on X and has sent out ​invites to select guests, according to some user posts,” Reuters reporter Abhirup Roy continued, adding that Tesla did not announce a time for the event as of yesterday.

Ford For The Win (For Now)

If Ford’s PR team really intended to stomp all over the Cybercab event, they did a pretty good job. They even staged a Las Vegas photoshoot and posted photos of a camouflaged Fathom on Elon Musk’s own social media platform, X (formerly Twitter), on September 1.

In addition to a lavish write-up in the Wall Street Journal, the Ford Fathom also earned a fresh round of attention in the Detroit Free Press on the eve of the Cybercab event, whatever that may be.

“Ford Motor Co. plans to officially reveal its new all-electric midsize pickup Fathom by year-end, but until then, CEO Jim Farley is teasing car buyers with peeks at it,” reported Jamie L. LaReau for the Free Press, referring to the photos posted on X.

“Farley, who has a background in marketing and was previously Ford’s head of marketing before becoming CEO in Oct. 2020, shared the photos to keep the buzz buzzing on this very important vehicle for the Dearborn-based automaker,” LaReau noted.

Just What Texas Needs: A Golden Cybercab

To be clear, the Ford Fathom and the Tesla Cybercab are aimed at two entirely different vehicle use cases. If Ford is to achieve maximum satisfaction from the Fathom, that would not involve outselling the Cybercab. It would probably mean eclipsing sales of the woebegone Telsa Cybertruck by a wide margin.

Still, the contrast between the two PR teams is eyebrow-raising. As Trump’s war in Iran drags on, affordability has become a key issue in the upcoming midterm elections, making fertile ground for an automaker to pitch a practical, everyday EV at a relatively reasonable starting price of just under $30,000 (the Free Press cites $29,945 to start, including the $1,595 delivery fee), suitable for both fleets and individual buyers.

The Cybercab also clocks in at around $30,000, but it’s difficult to see any use case materializing beyond fleets, with the further limitation that Musk is showcasing the car as a sort of golden chariot for the well-heeled. That may go over well in some places, but the affordability crisis has hit Texas households over the head with a Texas-sized fist, particularly in the area of housing.

Wither Robotaxis?

The gold-toned antics of the super-rich have not been doing so well right now, with President Trump himself slapping his Midas touch on every surface within reach. With that in mind, Musk’s decision to showcase exclusivity is tone-deaf, to put it kindly.

Be that as it may, the leadup to the Cybercab event is just the beginning salvo of a PR throwdown as Ford zeroes in on Tesla. As noted by the Free Press, the Ford Fathom is the first of five new EVs to be manufactured on the new Universal platform, with deliveries of the Fathom beginning next year.

Ford is also among the automakers hedging their EV bets with an EREV (Extended Range EV) option, an idea first pioneered by General Motors in the short-lived Chevy Volt back in the early 2000’s. Now everyone is doing it, with some notable exceptions including Rivian, the Jeff Bezos venture Slate Auto, and, of course, Tesla.

For its entry into the EREV pool, Ford is reviving the much-hyped Ford Lightning F-150 electric pickup truck with an onboard gas engine as a range extender, enabling travel of more than 700 miles. As with other EREVs, the vehicle runs on electricity all the time, with the engine and a generator kicking in to provide an additional kick when needed. Ford anticipates the pickup will appeal to EV fans who have long-distance towing on their agenda.

Ford initially pitched the original Lightning as a mobile power source in the event of grid outages and other emergencies, before halting production in December of 2025. Exportable electricity is likewise on the menu for the forthcoming  EREV version, so keep an eye out for that angle as Ford ramps up its marketing machine.

Photo: Ford has been carefully camouflaging prototypes of its forthcoming Ford Fathom electric pickup truck, but a Ford dealer in Texas has already begun teasing the look of a mid-sized pickup (cropped, courtesy of All Star Ford, Palestine, Texas).

data.title: Electric Car Batteries Hold Up Really Well — These Are “The Best”
data.description:
In general, there’s far more concern about electric car range and electric car battery longevity than there needs to be. We’ve got a 2019 Tesla Model 3 SR+ and a 2018 BMW i3 REx and just need to charge them up once or twice a week overnight at home. Electric cars on the market now have far, far more range, better batteries, and negligible concern about battery longevity.

Electric cars have like three to four times more range than they did a decade ago, so even if they see significant battery degradation, they are still going to have far more range than electric cars bought 10 years ago had!

Anyway, Aviloo, an EV diagnostics company, recently examined the batteries of a bunch of electric vehicles to see how well they held up after 50,000 km (31,068 miles), 100,000 km (62,137 miles), and 150,000 km (93,205 miles). They conducted 500,000+ battery health tests for this. Let’s take a look at the results and see who fared best.

Oh, also note that these tests spanned most continents — North America, South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia — and took place between 2022 and 2026. Also, of course, not all EV models were examined (that would be impossible). The company looked at just 20 popular models. So, we can see which models did the best from this group, but we don’t know which electric car models truly have the best medium-term and long-term battery performance.

So, as we can see, these electric car models largely had about 95% of their original battery capacity (or range) remaining after 50,000 km, and they were typically in the lower 90% after 150,000 km. Some of the cars tested had still only lost a few percent of their original capacity even after 150,000 km. However, some had lost about 20%, or even did so after about 100,000 km. Frankly, when we’re talking about hundreds of kilometers of original range, in my humble opinion, it really doesn’t matter or make much difference. Perhaps you charge a few more times in a month, and that takes a few seconds of actual activity on your part each time.

Some standout models, as you can see, are as follows:

  • Hyundai IONIQ 5
  • Hyundai Kona EV
  • Mercedes-Benz EQA
  • BMW i4
  • Volvo XC40 Recharge
  • Polestar 2
  • Ford Mustang Mach-E

Kudos to those models and brands, and congratulations to anyone who chose to buy them!

I won’t focus in on the models that did less well, but feel free to chime in down below with any thoughts you have on those, or on the top-performing models.
